etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English wrappen (“to wrap, fold”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to North Frisian wrappe (“to press into; stop up”), dialectal Danish vrappe (“to stuff, cram”), Middle Low German rincworpen (“to envelop, wrap”), Middle Low German wrempen (“to wrinkle, scrunch the face”), all perhaps tied to Proto-Indo-European *werp-, *werb- (“to turn, twist, bend”).

Compare also similar-sounding and similar-meaning Middle English wlappen (“to wrap, lap, envelop, fold”), Middle Dutch lappen (“to wrap up”), Old Italian goluppare (“to wrap”) (from Germanic). Doublet of lap; related to envelop, develop. Also compare Latin verber (“whip, lash”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To enclose (an object) completely in any flexible, thin material such as fabric or paper.

quote.citation: 1947, Harry Stephen Keeler, The Case of the Barking Clock:
quote.text: I then dried these over a flame, and then, wrapping the formes and re-sealing them with my court seals — for my only commission, you see, was to report as to whether the type was unpied, and text ungarbled, and the formes all ready  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To enclose or coil around an object or organism, as a form of grasping.

quote.text: Like one who wraps the drapery of his couch / About him, and lies down to pleasant dreams.

quote.citation: 2003, Gary Tigerman, The Orion Protocol, New York, N.Y.: William Morrow, →ISBN, page 143:
quote.text: The prehistoric caribou they had already liberated was wrapped in a space blanket and carefully tied to a sled. The Science Foundation team had then moved on to a deep translucent blue seam in the ice that proved to be a window on the rest of the ungulant herd standing poised in suspended animation, as if waiting for time to start again.

definitions.definition: (transitive, figurative) To conceal by enveloping or enfolding; to hide.

quote.citation: a. 1640, Thomas Carew, Ingrateful Beauty Threatened:
quote.text: wise poets that wrap truth in tales

definitions.definition: (transitive or intransitive, video production) To finish shooting (filming) a video, television show, or movie.
(transitive, lines, words, text, etc.) To break a continuous line (of text) onto the next line
(computing, transitive) To make functionality available through a software wrapper.
(transitive or intransitive) To (cause to) reset to an original value after passing a maximum.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English wrappe, from the verb (see above).

definitions.definition: Paper or sheeting that is wrapped around something to protect, contain, or conceal it.
A loose piece of women's clothing that one wraps around the body; a shawl or scarf.
(chiefly in the plural, now rare) An outer garment worn as protection while riding, travelling etc.

quote.citation: 1872, George Eliot, Middlemarch, Book I, chapter 6:
quote.text: ‘I see you have had our Lowick Cicero here,’ she said, seating herself comfortably, throwing back her wraps, and showing a thin but well-built figure.

definitions.definition: A type of food consisting of various ingredients wrapped in a tortilla or pancake.
(entertainment) The completion of all or a major part of a performance.

quote.text: But she could knock off right after the wrap, have dinner, and take a later flight.

quote.citation: 2003 January 12, “Encore Presentation: Interview With the Bee Gees”, in CNN_KingWknd:
quote.text: The first time I met him is when we went to the – after the wrap party, we went to a little sound room – or a little screening room and watched the preview
And that's a wrap on "News Watch." For Judy, Jim, Cal and Kirsten, I'm Jon Scott. We'll see you again next week.'

definitions.definition: (television, radio) A complete news report ready for broadcast, incorporating spoken reporting and other material.

quote.citation: 2005, Alan R. Stephenson, David E. Reese, Mary E. Beadle, Broadcast Announcing Worktext, page 164:
quote.text: This is a news report from the scene of the event. When a voicer and an actuality are combined into one complete story, it's known as a wrap.

quote.citation: 2005, Ted White, Broadcast News: Writing, Reporting, and Producing, page 245:
quote.text: Attend a news conference, and prepare a wrap or package.
